item.title: Beyond alcohol cue reactivity: A novel test of task-based event-related potentials as a measure of individual differences in natural reward cue processing in alcohol use disorder
item.description:
Background: Incentive salience attribution (ISA) is the process by which reward-associated cues take value themselves. Translational work has observed individual ISA differences that predict behavior - suggesting prognostic potential for alcohol/substance use disorders. With human basic science observing ISA differences with natural reward (e.g., food) cues, this study tested if natural reward (rather than disorder-triggering) cues can also be used to assess ISA in alcohol use disorder (AUD).

Method: 30 individuals with AUD and heavy drinking at screening did a validated task wherein pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral content-depicting pictures were seen along with 1) low-salience cues that predicted M&M rewards, and 2) alcohol-related comparator images. To capture ISA heterogeneity as before, k-means clustering was applied to an electroencephalographic late positive potential (LPP) salience index.

Results: As in prior work, clustering identified "Cue > Pleasant" (C>P; n = 14) and "Cue < Pleasant" (C<P; n = 16) groups who showed enhanced or reduced LPPs for reward-predicting cues relative to pleasant-depicting pictures. Beyond cue responding, C>P and C<P groups each showed enhancement for pleasant and unpleasant, compared to neutral, pictures and did not show LPP enhancement - but did show enhanced earlier P300 - for alcohol images. Finally, groups did not differ in task-based M&M consumption or average weekly drinking but did differ in drinking recency (more C<P individuals drank within 2 days of their session).

Conclusions: Results 1) provide proof-of-concept for assessing ISA in AUD without cuing alcohol, and 2) motivate further work to fully test predictiveness of disorder-relevant variables (e.g., drinking during alcohol availability; treatment outcomes).

Sege CT, Walton RM, Hahn AM, LaPorta S, McTeague LM

item.title: "He's a social creature… he just had no one to share anything with." Social isolation among deaths attributed to acute stimulant toxicity in San Francisco, CA
item.description:
Background: Notwithstanding data suggesting social isolation may play a role in mortality from acute drug toxicity, few studies have explicitly explored the association.

Methods: We analyzed qualitative data from a mixed methods psychological autopsy study of 101 deaths attributed to stimulants in San Francisco, CA. Sociodemographic measures and drugs involved in death were obtained from death records. Interviews were conducted with 141 informants and transcribed and coded using a qualitative codebook. We conducted a thematic analysis of interview excerpts related to loneliness and social isolation.

Results: We identified three interconnected themes: social isolation following major life changes or traumatic events, the bidirectional relationship between social isolation and substance use, and social isolation proximal to death. Informants described decedent isolation as both a driver and consequence of stimulant use. Social isolation was exacerbated by major life changes and anticipated stigma. Many informants described decedents using substances alone due to isolation or feelings of shame, which precluded the presence of a bystander able to respond to their fatal event.

Conclusion: We found that social isolation played a major role in stimulant deaths in our sample. Social isolation both contributed to and resulted from stimulant use and associated stigma and shame. Efforts to prevent stimulant deaths should prioritize reducing isolation and strengthening social connection through nonjudgemental environments.

Chang YG, McMahan VM, Muñiz MA, Marti XL, Gundy G, Rodda LN

item.title: Impulse control as a mediator between mental health and substance use across diverse adolescent and young adult samples
item.description:
Background: Substance use (SU) and substance use disorders (SUD) are common and often co-occur with psychopathology including depression, anxiety, and emotional dysregulation (ED). The specific role of ED components, including impulsivity, and their links to various substances has not been fully studied. This research examines how impulse control relates to anxiety, depression, and SU in adolescents and young adults (AYA).

Methods: The study involved baseline data from 1246 participants aged 14-30 (M=20.07, SD=4.48) from behavioral health clinics, juvenile justice, juvenile rehabilitation, and high schools across four projects focused on opioid and other SU prevention. Analyses tested whether impulse control challenges mediated the indirect effects of depression and anxiety on SU (alcohol, cannabis, opioids).

Results: We fitted group structural mediation models in which mental health factors (depression or anxiety) predicted impulse control, which in turn predicted SU (alcohol, cannabis, opioids). Generally, AYA with high depression or anxiety had higher SU rates for alcohol and cannabis, and the associations were partly mediated by challenges in impulse control.

Conclusion: AYA with depression or anxiety are more likely to exhibit increased impulsivity and SU, and impulsivity further raised the risk of SU among those with depression or anxiety. Hence, careful monitoring of symptoms related to anxiety, depression, and impulsivity may help identify AYA at the highest risk for developing problematic SU and SUD.

Shelley LT, Yule AM, Wilens TE, Morgan-López AA, Ridenour TA, Stone M

item.title: Fentanyl and xylazine precipitated withdrawal in Swiss Webster mice
item.description:
Background: In recent years, α2-adrenoreceptor (α2AR) agonists have become common adulterants of illicit fentanyl supplies. One such drug is xylazine, a veterinary anesthetic not approved for human use. There is little known about effects of xylazine upon repeated administration, interactions between fentanyl and xylazine, and how xylazine may alter withdrawal from fentanyl. In this work, we established a precipitated withdrawal procedure with the goal of understanding withdrawal from xylazine and how it may impact withdrawal from fentanyl.

Methods: Mice received fentanyl, xylazine, or both, followed by antagonists naloxone, idazoxan, or both 2h later. Mice were then placed into a large glass beaker and observed for two 60s intervals at 9- and 17-min post injection, and presence of withdrawal signs was recorded in each interval.

Results: Injections of fentanyl or xylazine followed by antagonists naloxone or idazoxan, respectively, each produced a unique set of precipitated withdrawal signs. Both produced significant grimace and wet dog shakes; however, precipitated fentanyl withdrawal also produced paw tremors and jumps whereas xylazine withdrawal produced scratching. Xylazine coadministration with fentanyl increased the frequency of some signs of fentanyl precipitated withdrawal while decreasing others.

Conclusion: This work suggests that the addition of xylazine to illicit fentanyl supplies is changing the somatic state of fentanyl withdrawal, which may impact patients in clinical settings.

Shepherd B, Cakir K, Walker EA

item.title: Perceived sleep disruption and opioid consumption in chronic low back pain: Craving as a mediating pathway
item.description:
Background: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) affects more than 600 million people worldwide, many of whom receive long-term opioid therapy (LTOT). Sleep disturbance, particularly wake after sleep onset (WASO), may contribute to opioid craving and use, yet the temporal relationships among WASO, craving, and opioid dose in chronic pain populations remain poorly understood.

Methods: Adults with CLBP receiving LTOT (N = 81) completed 14 days of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and overnight actigraphy monitoring. WASO was assessed using sleep diaries and overnight actigraphy, while morning and nocturnal craving, pain severity, and daily opioid dose (morphine milligram equivalents) were assessed using EMA. Linear mixed-effects models examined main and interactive effects of WASO and pain severity on craving and opioid dose. Multilevel mediation models tested whether craving mediated the relationship between WASO and opioid dose.

Results: Greater diary-based WASO was associated with higher nocturnal opioid craving. Pain severity emerged as a strong predictor of both nocturnal and morning craving and moderated the association between WASO and opioid dose, such that greater WASO was associated with higher opioid dose on high-pain days. Mediation analyses demonstrated significant indirect effects of WASO on opioid dose through both nocturnal and morning craving. Exploratory analyses using actigraphy-derived WASO showed minimal associations with craving or opioid dose.

Conclusions: Perceived sleep disruption was associated with opioid craving and opioid consumption among individuals with CLBP receiving LTOT. Craving may represent a cognitive-affective pathway linking disrupted sleep to opioid use, highlighting sleep disturbance as a potentially modifiable intervention target in chronic pain populations.

Towers EB, Denoue C, Reid MJ, Thrul J, Huhn AS, Dunn KE
